title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
short: With no outside torque Iω stays the same, so a skater who pulls in her arms spins faster.
trouble: Students think the skater's kinetic energy stays the same when she pulls her arms in; it grows, because she does work.

blocks.html: An angular impulse $\tau\Delta t$ changes angular momentum. So when no outside torque acts, angular momentum cannot change at all, which explains spinning skaters, divers, and why planets speed up near the Sun.

If the net outside torque on a system is zero, its angular momentum stays the same: $$\role[rotational inertia before]{mass}{I_1}\role[spin rate before]{angvel}{\omega_1} = \role[rotational inertia after]{mass}{I_2}\role[spin rate after]{angvel}{\omega_2}.$$ Pull mass toward the axis (smaller $I$) and the spin speeds up; push it outward and the spin slows.

Inside a system, every force has a third-law partner, equal, opposite and along the same line, so their torques cancel. Only outside torques can change the total $L$. A skater on smooth ice feels almost no torque about her vertical axis, so her $L$ is fixed. Her kinetic energy is not: writing $K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$, the same $L$ with a smaller $I$ means a bigger $K$. The extra energy comes from the work her arms do pulling the weights inward, against their tendency to keep moving in a straight line.

blocks.name: ph-rotation

opts.task: Slide the arms in. $L$ (teal) stays put while $\omega$ and $K$ grow.

blocks.cap: A skater pulls in two weights: $I$ drops, $\omega$ rises and $L = I\omega$ stays the same.

blocks.title: A skater pulls in her arms
blocks.q: A skater spins at $1.5\ \text{rev/s}$ with $I = 4.5\ \text{kg·m}^2$. She pulls in her arms, reducing $I$ to $1.5\ \text{kg·m}^2$. Find her new spin rate and the change in her kinetic energy.
steps: $K_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}(4.5)(9.42)^2 = 200\ \text{J}$; $K_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.5)(28.3)^2 = 600\ \text{J}$. Three times as much: her arms did $400\ \text{J}$ of work.

blocks.title: A disk dropped on a turntable
blocks.q: A turntable ($I = 0.020\ \text{kg·m}^2$) spins freely at $45$ rpm. A disk with $I = 0.010\ \text{kg·m}^2$, not spinning, is dropped on it, centered. Find the final rate.
steps: Friction between them is internal: $I_1\omega_1 = (I_1 + I_2)\omega_f$.
Like a sticking collision: angular momentum is kept, but kinetic energy drops (to two thirds here).

blocks.title: Jumping on a merry-go-round
blocks.q: A $30\ \text{kg}$ child runs at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$ along a line tangent to the edge of a resting merry-go-round (a uniform disk, $120\ \text{kg}$, radius $2.0\ \text{m}$) and jumps on at the rim. Find $\omega$ afterward.

blocks.html: Thinking the skater's kinetic energy stays the same when she pulls her arms in. Angular momentum is what stays the same; kinetic energy grows, because $K = L^2/2I$ and $I$ shrinks. Conservation of one quantity doesn't mean conservation of the other, just as momentum but not kinetic energy survives a sticking collision. Check: pulling arms in takes effort, so energy must be going in.
